title: Staffing mix in veterinary services: administrative support is about 22% of jobs but projected to grow far slower than clinical roles

history.reason: Weak signal only: BLS employment-matrix data show the staffing mix and projections but no measure of administrative workload. AVMA reports and BLS Occupational Outlook pages were not readable (bot-blocked) and were not used.

description: BLS data show office and administrative support makes up about 22% of employment in veterinary services and is projected to grow about 1.0% from 2025 to 2035, versus about 9.9% for veterinarians, technicians and assistants. Whether independent practices carry an unmet administrative or non-clinical workload is not established by these sources.
customer_segment: Veterinary services employers (NAICS 541940), including independent practices; the data do not separate independent from corporate-owned practices.
context: Scoping record built from federal statistics. AVMA workforce and economic reports and the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook returned bot-protection or access-denied pages to automated clients and were not bypassed, so no workload or burnout survey was read. This record does not show a customer problem.

evidence.text: BLS reports veterinary services employment of 473.6 thousand in 2025, of which office and administrative support is 105.9 thousand (22.4%) and receptionists and information clerks are 55.6 thousand (11.7%).
BLS projects 2025-2035 employment growth of 9.9% for veterinarians, veterinary technicians and veterinary assistants but 1.0% for office and administrative support in veterinary services.
BLS reports 7.2% of veterinarians (6.6 thousand of 91.1 thousand) are self-employed in 2025.

APHIS estimates 1.0 hour per NVAP application response, with 22,581 annual respondents and 22,582 responses (22,582 burden hours per year); NVAP is voluntary and this covers the application form only.
Slow projected growth of administrative staff alongside faster clinical growth could mean more non-clinical tasks fall on clinical staff or need to be automated.

alternatives: Practice-management software, outsourced billing and call-answering services, and corporate group back offices: not investigated.

contradictory_evidence.text: The data are employment counts and projections; they show no administrative burden, vacancy or overtime, and a projection of slow growth may reflect forecasting assumptions (for example technology) rather than shortage.

The only administrative task read, the voluntary NVAP application, is estimated by APHIS at 1.0 hour per application response; this is an agency PRA estimate for application respondents only, not observed time and not a recurring annual duty for every veterinarian, and it says little about overall practice administrative burden.
Veterinary services includes corporate-owned practices whose back-office staff may be counted differently; independent-practice staffing cannot be isolated.
BLS and APHIS are statistical or administering agencies, not parties selling solutions, but neither measured workload.

uncertainty: Unknown: time clinicians and managers spend on administrative work, vacancy and turnover rates for front-office roles, independent versus corporate staffing, which tasks cause pain, and willingness to pay. Data are 2025 base and 2035 projections with release date not read.
open_questions: Do AVMA or state veterinary association surveys (if readable) quantify administrative or front-office workload and turnover?
How do staffing ratios differ between independent and corporate practices?
Which non-clinical tasks (records, client communication, billing, controlled-substance logs) consume the most staff time?
next_actions: Find a readable primary survey on veterinary practice staffing and administrative time (AVMA report PDFs if accessible by normal means, state veterinary medical associations, or peer-reviewed studies).
Do not treat this record as a validated problem until workload or turnover evidence is read.
